alerts.headline: Winter Storm Warning issued November 18 at 5:19PM PST until November 20 at 4:00AM PST by NWS Hanford CA
alerts.description:
* WHAT...Heavy snow. Total snow accumulations between 1 to 3 feet
expected above this elevation; accumulations around 4 feet above
8,000 feet. Winds could gust as high as 45 mph.

* WHERE...Sierra Nevada above 5,000 feet.

* WHEN...Until 4 AM PST Friday.

* IMPACTS...Travel could be very difficult to impossible. The
hazardous conditions will impact daily travel. Gusty winds could
bring down tree branches. Roads, and especially bridges and
overpasses, will likely become slick and hazardous.
alerts.instruction:
If you must travel, keep an extra flashlight, food, and water in your
vehicle in case of an emergency. The latest road conditions for the
state you are calling from can be obtained by calling 5 1 1.

Persons should consider delaying all travel. If travel is absolutely
necessary, drive with extreme caution. Consider taking a winter storm
kit along with you, including such items as tire chains, booster
cables, flashlight, shovel, blankets and extra clothing. Also take
water, a first aid kit, and anything else that would help you survive
in case you become stranded.
alerts.areas: Yosemite NP outside of the valley; San Joaquin River Canyon; Upper San Joaquin River; Kaiser to Rodgers Ridge; Kings Canyon NP; Grant Grove Area; Sequoia NP; South End of the Upper Sierra

alerts.headline: Flood Advisory issued November 18 at 5:11PM PST until November 18 at 7:15PM PST by NWS Sacramento CA
alerts.description:
* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues.

* WHERE...Portions of Colusa, Placer, Sacramento, Solano, Sutter,
Yolo, and Yuba Counties in California...


* WHEN...Until 715 PM PST.

* IMPACTS...Minor flooding in low-lying and poor drainage areas.
Water over roadways. Ponding of water in urban or other areas is
occurring or is imminent.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 508 PM PST, Doppler radar and automated rain gauges
indicated heavy rain. Minor flooding is ongoing or expected
to begin shortly in the advisory area. Between 1 and 2 inches
of rain have fallen.
- Some locations that will experience flooding include...
Sacramento, Elk Grove, Roseville, Vallejo, Fairfield,
Vacaville, Citrus Heights, Folsom, Davis, Rocklin, Woodland,
Marysville, Carmichael, Fair Oaks, Yuba City, Rancho Cordova,
West Sacramento, Lincoln, Suisun City and Dixon.
- Includes portions of Interstate 80, Highway 50, Interstate 5
and Highway 99
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
alerts.instruction:
Turn around, don't drown when encountering flooded roads. Most flood
deaths occur in vehicles.

Be especially cautious at night when it is harder to recognize the
dangers of flooding.

Please report observed flooding to local emergency services or law
enforcement and request they pass this information to the National
Weather Service when you can do so safely.

AREA FORECAST DISCUSSION
National Weather Service Eureka CA
345 PM PST Wed Nov 18 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

* Widespread frost and areas of freezing temperatures Friday and
  Saturday mornings.

* A colder storm will arrive over the weekend.

* Breezy winds and light, lower elevation snow with the weekend 
  storm. 

* Weather pattern to likely remain active next week.

&&

.SYNOPSIS...Showers will continue behind the latest front. Much 
colder air develops Friday and Saturday mornings. The next colder 
storm system brings better chances for lower mountain snowfall, 
moderate to heavy rain, and some gusty southerly winds. The 
pattern looks to remain active next week and possible through the 
holiday. 


&&

.DISCUSSION...After a night and morning of strong southerly winds, 
some heavy rainfall, and mountain snow, quieter conditions 
developed. Light rain and some showers linger behind the front, 
and chances of showers will continue. The threat for snowfall over
Trinity County will also end early Thursday morning.

The chances for frost outside of Trinity, Lake, and interior 
Mendocino counties, where the growing season ended, will be 
limited tonight due to the shower activity associated cloudcover. 
Better clearing will develop Thursday night. There are still some 
questions with stratus coverage along the coast, mainly around 
Humboldt Bay. Outside of any areas of stratus of patchy fog, 
widespread areas will see temperatures drop will likely drop to 
frost and freeing levels. Cold weather Advisory conditions may be 
met, but much will depend on how fast cloudcover actually clears 
out. 

A dynamic trough with high instability will be moving ashore 
through Central CA tonight through Thursday. Strong thunderstorms 
are forecast for areas south of Lake and Mendcino County, but these 
far southern areas, including along the coast, will still need to be 
watched for thunderstorm activity or heavier rainfall rates into 
Thursday morning.   

The next weather system will begin the impact the region early 
Saturday morning. The colder air described in place will allow for 
snow at lower elevations than the previous front. Trapped cold air 
over Trinity County will also keep snow levels lower as 
precipitation spreads in, which currently look to drop snow levels 
down to 2000 ft, or possible lower. A Winter Weather Advisory will 
be likely needed, and possible Winter Storm Warning if total 
forecast precipitation increases. Southerly winds will be gusty, but 
look to stay below advisory levels. 

Moderate to locally heavy rainfall will quickly pass through 
Saturday with the front. There are high chances (70 to 80%) for over 
an inch of rain for mainly areas closer to the coast Saturday, and 
these probabilities quickly lower inland. There are moderate (30 
to 40%) chances for gusts over 35 mph for the coastal areas and 
exposed headlands, but high chances for gusts over 30 mph. There 
will be stronger high elevation winds above 3500 ft, so there will
be stronger ridgetop winds. 

The extended pattern continues to look active next week and
possibly through the holiday. Rainfall may extend into Monday 
from a clipping system the north to start. Come Tuesday, 60% of 
the clusters have 1 to 2 inches of rainfall in a 24 hour period, 
and 80% of clusters on Wednesday. Beyond some increasing flooding
risks, the standout threat continues to be the coastal flooding 
threat from high astronomical tides and tidal anomaly that will 
coincide with the storms, and the southerly winds and larger surf 
which would likely accompany the storms. See the Coastal Flooding 
section below. 


&&

.AVIATION...Sporadic post frontal showers are heavy at times in the 
northern sector of coastal del Norte, KCEC specifically. Moderate to 
heavy rain and gusts could affect approach at least until 02-03z 
this evening at KCEC but likely only MVFR or low end IFR at the 
lowest flight minimums as ceilings hover around 4500-6000ft. Models 
have rain tapering off around 03z with improved conditions by 
Thursday. KACV is a bit more predictable and steady with VFR 
conditions continuing through the TAF period. Southerly winds turn 
east-northeast this evening for KCEC and KACV, helping clear things 
out a bit. KUKI has had a decent amount of rainfall, most of it 
ending by 16z but vicinity showers remain through Thursday 
afternoon. VFR at KUKI until tonight when RRFS model shows Mendocino 
area ceilings coming down to around 2200-2600ft...MVFR soon after 
those ceilings come down. /EYS


&&

.MARINE...Winds have backed off considerably after this mornings 
chaotic, hazardous, and water-spout/near tornadic conditions off of 
the coast which included a special marine warning. Steep seas 
continue with the buoys reporting 14ft at 13seconds as the swell 
diminishes but only slightly as energetic waves still linger for the 
next 24 hours. Small craft advisories are out for all area waters 
until late night Thursday/ early Friday morning with most of the 
hazard continuing in the southern inner and outer zones. /EYS


&&

.COASTAL FLOODING...High astronomical tides arrive this weekend, 
lasting into next week. Astronomical tides reaches 6.19 ft above 
MLLW by Thursday 11/19 and 7.20 ft at the North Spit tide gauge by 
Saturday 11/21.

The tidal anomaly has been reading consistently over 1.5 feet due to 
higher than normal ocean temperatures from El Nino's effect. Storm 
surge lately has added as much as an additional 1.5 ft. These two 
factors have already once compounded to create a total anomaly of
3.0 feet. With high forecast certainty of the storm track 
continuing over the area through the next 2 weeks, high tidal 
anomalies are likely to continue. Minor flooding around Humboldt 
Bay (water levels above 8.8 ft MLLW) is likely as soon this this 
coming weekend. The highest astronomical tides for November is 
between 11/24 and 11/26 with each day reaching above 8.4 ft. 
Should the 1.5 ft anomaly remain, which it appears likely, 9.9 ft 
tide levels are possible. The current record tide level is 10.37 
ft MLLW set earlier this year. Should we have a storm, which at 
this point appears likely, there exists a chance for record 
breaking tide levels causing moderate to major flooding. Potential
high surf with these storm systems would greatly amplify the 
hazard risk for much of the coast during the high tides. 


&&

A STRONG STORM SYSTEM CONTINUES TO MOVE THROUGH THE AREA TODAY 
THROUGH EARLY FRIDAY MORNING BRINGING HEAVY MOUNTAIN SNOW, STRONG
SOUTH TO SOUTHEASTERLY WINDS, WIDESPREAD PRECIPITATION, AND 
ISOLATED THUNDERSTORM CHANCES. THE BULK OF THE PRECIPITATION WILL 
MOVE THROUGH TODAY THROUGH THURSDAY MORNING. LINGERING LIGHT 
SHOWERS EXPECTED FRIDAY, BEFORE PREDOMINANTLY DRY WEATHER RETURNS 
LATER IN THE DAY.

MODERATE TO HEAVY SNOW IS EXPECTED MAINLY OVER THE SIERRA AND
SOUTHERN CASCADES WITH HOURLY RATES OF 1 TO 2+ INCHES. THE

BRIEFLY DOWN TO 3500 FEET EARLY FRIDAY MORNING. TOTAL SNOWFALL 
AMOUNTS ARE BETWEEN 2 TO 4 FEET ABOVE 5000 FEET, WITH UP TO 5 FEET
AT THE HIGHEST PEAKS. 6 TO 15 INCHES ARE EXPECTED BETWEEN 
4000-5000 FEET, AND A DUSTING TO MINOR ACCUMULATIONS OF SNOW AS 
LOW AS 3000 FEET. WINDS ARE FORECAST TO GUST AS HIGH AS 60 MPH, 
WHICH MAY RESULT IN NEAR WHITEOUT CONDITIONS AND SIGNIFICANT 
REDUCTIONS IN VISIBILITY AT TIMES. 

A WINTER STORM WARNING CONTINUES UNTIL 4 AM THURSDAY FOR THE 
COAST RANGE AND SHASTA COUNTY MOUNTAINS ABOVE 4000 FEET; AND 
UNTIL 4 AM FRIDAY FOR THE SOUTHERN CASCADES AND SIERRA ABOVE 4000 
FEET. TRAVEL COULD BE VERY DIFFICULT TO IMPOSSIBLE THROUGH EARLY 
FRIDAY MORNING. IF YOU MUST TRAVEL OVER THE MOUNTAINS, ALWAYS 
CARRY A WINTER SAFETY KIT AND MAKE SURE TO CHECK 
QUICKMAP.CA.DOT.GOV FOR THE LATEST ROAD CONDITIONS.


...RAIN IMPACTS... 
MULTIPLE WAVES OF PRECIPITATION WILL CONTINUE TO MOVE ACROSS 
INTERIOR NORTHERN CALIFORNIA TODAY THROUGH THURSDAY. THE HEAVIEST
PRECIPITATION IS EXPECTED THROUGH THIS AFTERNOON, AND AGAIN 
OVERNIGHT TONIGHT THROUGH EARLY THURSDAY MORNING. PERIODS OF 
MODERATE TO HEAVY RAIN MOVING INTO THE VALLEY HAVE ALREADY 
RESULTED IN MINOR ROADWAY AND URBAN FLOODING. THESE ONGOING 
CONDITIONS WILL MAKE THE EVENING COMMUTE DIFFICULT. THE THREAT 
FOR ADDITIONAL MINOR FLOODING IMPACTS CONTINUES OVERNIGHT AS 
ANOTHER ROUND OF HEAVIER PRECIPITATION MOVES THROUGH. THE BULK OF 
THE PRECIPITATION IS FORECAST TO EXIT THE VALLEY BY LATE THURSDAY 
MORNING, RESULTING IN CLEARER CONDITIONS AND ADDITIONAL CHANCES 
FOR THUNDERSTORMS. PRECIPITATION WILL CONTINUE TO LINGER OVER THE 
FOOTHILLS THROUGH THURSDAY AFTERNOON, BEFORE MORE WIDESPREAD DRY 
WEATHER RETURNS ON FRIDAY.

ADDITIONALLY, A FLOOD ADVISORY IS IN EFFECT UNTIL 4:45 PM FRIDAY
FOR LOW-LYING AREAS ALONG THE SAN PABLO BAY, CARQUINEZ STRAIT, AND
SUISUN BAY SHORELINES IN SOLANO COUNTY, AS WELL AS LOW-LYING AREAS
ALONG THE SACRAMENTO RIVER, SAN JOAQUIN RIVER, AND OTHER DELTA
WATERWAYS. THIS IS DUE TO THE POTENTIAL FOR COASTAL FLOODING AS A
RESULT OF STORM INDUCED HIGHER TIDES.


...THUNDERSTORM POTENTIAL...
ISOLATED THUNDERSTORMS WILL BE POSSIBLE WEDNESDAY AND THURSDAY,
DURING THE AFTERNOON/EVENING HOURS AND EARLY THURSDAY MORNING.
GREATEST THUNDERSTORM POTENTIAL EXISTS ON THURSDAY AS CONDITIONS
CLEAR IN THE VALLEY BEHIND THE SYSTEM. ADDITIONALLY THERE WILL BE
A BRIEF WINDOW WHERE STRONG SPEED SHEAR AND INSTABILITY ALIGN
THURSDAY AFTERNOON, BRINGING THE POTENTIAL FOR A FEW STRONG TO 
SEVERE THUNDERSTORMS WHICH MAY GENERATE QUARTER SIZE HAIL AND/OR 
THE LOW CHANCE FOR A BRIEF TORNADO.

...WIND IMPACTS...
ADDITIONALLY, A WIND ADVISORY REMAINS IN EFFECT UNTIL 10 PM 
TONIGHT FOR THE DELTA, SACRAMENTO AND NORTHERN SAN JOAQUIN 
VALLEYS, AND ADJACENT FOOTHILLS. SOUTH TO SOUTHEAST WINDS 20 TO 30
MPH ARE EXPECTED, WITH GUSTS AS HIGH AS 55 MPH. WINDS WILL
CONTINUE TO BE STRONG THROUGH THE AFTERNOON BEFORE GRADUALLY
WEAKENING THROUGH THE EVENING. 


...THE WEEKEND SYSTEM... 
ANOTHER STORM SYSTEM WILL APPROACH THE REGION THIS WEEKEND, 
BRINGING ADDITIONAL MOUNTAIN SNOW AND PRECIPITATION TO THE VALLEY.
PRECIPITATION AMOUNTS ARE STILL UNCERTAIN, BUT CONFIDENCE IS HIGH
THAT THIS STORM SYSTEM WILL HAVE LOWER PRECIPITATION AMOUNTS 
COMPARED TO THIS PREVIOUS SYSTEM. BE PREPARED TO MODIFY ANY 
THANKSGIVING TRAVEL PLANS OVER THE MOUNTAINS ACCORDINGLY AND STAY
UP TO DATE WITH THE LATEST FORECAST.


...WEEK OF THANKSGIVING...
DRIER WEATHER RESUMES ON MONDAY WITH COOLER TEMPERATURES. LATEST

.KEY MESSAGES...
Updated at 145 PM PST Wed Nov 18 2026

 - Strong winds, moderate to heavy rainfall at times with 
   isolated thunderstorms through Thursday afternoon

 - Hazardous beach conditions with high surf expected through 
   early Friday

 - Coastal flooding during high tides for areas adjacent to the 
   San Francisco and San Pablo Bays

 - Potential for impactful weather continues beyond the current 
   extended forecast

&&

.SHORT TERM...
Issued at 145 PM PST Wed Nov 18 2026
(This evening through Thursday night)

The cold front has cleared San Francisco and the North Bay at 
this hour and continued to drop southward across the region. We 
have seen rainfall heaviest in the coastal ranges of up to 0.5"-1"
at times along and ahead of the boundary. The cold front will 
continue to move southward across the Central Coast this afternoon
and early evening. Winds are drastically diminishing in wake of 
the front. Thus, we have canceled the Wind Advisory for coastal 
North Bay and will let the one for the East Bay Valleys and High 
Wind Warning for the East Bay Hills to expire at 1 PM. Meanwhile, 
we have added much of the Bay Area and Central Coast to a be 
included in the Wind Advisory through 4 PM this afternoon. While 
southerly winds will generally remain between 20 and 30 mph with 
gusts up to 50 mph in the advised area, higher gusts up to 70 mph 
will be possible in the higher terrain. 

In wake of the frontal passage, winds will ease regionwide and 
become more westerly or southwesterly. In the post-frontal 
environment, expecting widely scattered showers to persist with 
isolated thunderstorms as the colder air mass drops in from the 
north. Winds increase late tonight and into Thursday with the 
potential for additional Wind Advisories as the core of a surface 
low pressure moves into the region Thursday morning. As this 
occurs, SBCAPE values range from from 250-650 J/kg, leading to an 
increased threat of heavy downpours and thunderstorms capable of 
producing copious amounts of small (generally less than pea size) 
hail. The thunderstorm potential diminishes after sunset with the 
loss of daytime heating, yet rain showers look to persist into 
Friday morning. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
Issued at 145 PM PST Wed Nov 18 2026
(Friday through next Tuesday)

Temperatures are forecast to cool once again both Friday and 
Saturday mornings into the low-to-mid 30s in the North and East Bay 
Valleys as well as the southern Salinas Valley as colder air from 
the north settles into the region and winds ease. However, any cloud 
cover may result in warmer temperatures in those regions. Elsewhere, 
temperatures are forecast to be in the 40s those nights. 

Another cold front is forecast to approach the region on Saturday as 
a low pressure system approaches the Pacific Northwest. Rainfall 
from this system through Sunday is forecast to be significantly less 
than this current system.

Another system is forecast the days leading up to the Thanksgiving 
Holiday, but details are difficult to nail down 6-7 days out. Thus, 
remember to keep up-to-date with the latest forecast information.

&&

.AVIATION...
(00Z TAFS)
Issued at 409 PM PST Wed Nov 18 2026

Rain continues through the rest of the day into tomorrow 
morning and is replaced with scattered showers. The rain means 
widespread MVFR with isolated IFR as local heavy showers or low 
ceilings roll through. Our generally southerly winds have weakened 
since the morning and hang on until the low pressure center moves 
through later tonight into early tomorrow morning shifting us to 
stronger westerly winds. The scattered showers have the potential to 
form thunderstorms today and tomorrow, particularly in the 12z-18 
timeframe, with moderate to heavy rain and gusty winds possible.

2. A Winter Storm Warning for the Sierra Nevada above 5,000

with a marginal risk for severe thunderstorms in portions of 
the San Joaquin Valley, Sierra Nevada foothills, west side 
hills, and Yosemite NP.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Latest radar shows the initial band of precipitation over our
northern counties, with heavier shows from the SF Bay Area
northeastward. This band will continue to gradually move
southward through today and tonight.

The primary concern focuses on today until tomorrow in terms of
active weather. First, moderate to heavy rainfall will occur at
locations below 5,000 feet for much of the region. Second, heavy
snow takes place above 5,000 feet in the Sierra Nevada from
Yosemite NP to Tulare County. Lesser snow accumulations will
fall over the mountains to the south. Third, gusty winds will
continue until late this afternoon in the northern counties of
our forecast area, including much of Fresno County northward, 
in the San Joaquin Valley, Sierra foothills, and the west side 
hills. Gusty winds will also shift further southward by later
today and will occur until Thursday afternoon, including the west
side hills from Highway 198 southward to Kern County as we head
into later this afternoon. Finally, we are looking at
thunderstorms later today and another round on Thursday, when
the strongest storms are expected.

In terms of thunderstorms on Thursday, the Storm Prediction
Center (SPC) shows most of our counties under a Marginal Risk 
for severe thunderstorms. The threats include, a 2% chance of
isolated tornadoes, strong wind gusts of 60 mph or greater, and
small accumulating hail. Also, any thunderstorms are capable of
heavy rainfall and frequent dangerous lightning. Please note
that confidence is low regarding the possibility of any severe
weather, including severe thunderstorms and tornadoes. There are
some mitigating factors in play, such as how long the cloud 
cover will last into Thursday. In addition, temperatures will 
be mainly in the lower 60s at the warmest locations, and days 
are relatively short this time of year.

Besides the wind and thunderstorm threats, there remains a high
probability of one to three inches of rain in much of our area
at elevations up to 5,000 feet, one to three feet of snow in 
the Sierra Nevada from 5,000 to 8,000 feet, and three to four 
feet above 8,000 feet from now until Thursday night. The Kern
County desert currently has a 50-60 percent chance of half an 
inch of rainfall for the duration, although mainly on Thursday.

Another storm arrives late Saturday night and produces chances
of mainly light precipitation until Sunday evening. Chances of
precipitation are much lower, as uncertainty remains on the
exact locations. For now, there is at least a slight chance of
precipitation over much of our region.

Looking ahead, we are looking at increasing chances for yet
another storm on Tuesday and next Wednesday, or just in time for
Thanksgiving travel. As of now, the best chances of
precipitation will be Tuesday afternoon until Wednesday 
morning. More to follow soon!

.SYNOPSIS...
Cool weather will continue for the next week. Rain, isolated 
thunderstorms, high mountain snow, and stronger winds are 
expected Thursday as a storm system moves through California. Dry
but cool weather will follow Friday through Sunday. The next 
system looks weaker and could bring light rain Sunday night and 
Monday, potentially followed by another one mid to late next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...FOR EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA INCLUDING ORANGE...
SAN DIEGO...WESTERN RIVERSIDE AND SOUTHWESTERN SAN BERNARDINO
COUNTIES...


...UPDATED AVIATION/BEACHES/MARINE DISCUSSION...

.SHORT TERM...Wed Nov 18 through Thu Nov 19...Broad cyclonic flow
is currently present over the region, leading to weak onshore
winds and cool temperatures this afternoon. Skinny cumulus clouds
around 5000 feet this afternoon are indicative of a little bit of
moisture in the mid-levels; meanwhile, upper level clouds above
20k feet are starting to stream into the region ahead of a robust
cold front that will move through the region Thursday.

A mid-level low pressure center currently offshore of northern
California/Oregon will move slightly southwest to cover the CA/OR
border, sending a quick-moving, well-defined cold front through
southwest California with the southeast edge of the low. As this
approaches, winds will increase over the mountain ridges late
tonight into early Thursday morning. These winds will become more
widespread across the mountains into parts of the desert late
Thursday morning into the early afternoon with the main frontal
band, with peak gusts 45 to 60 mph over the mountain ridges into
the deserts foothills as well as through the mountain passes.
Winds will also become breezy for the valleys and coast as the
front passes, with peak gusts 15 to 30 mph.

As for rain, the vast majority of rain associated with this front
will fall Thursday morning and afternoon. While light, pre- 
frontal rain is possible for northern Orange County/IE as early as
about 7 AM, the main impactful band looks to hit the far northern
reach of our region (northern OC and IE) around 10 AM, then
far northwest San Diego County around 1 PM. This will bring
widespread moderate to heavy rain as it passes through. Warm ocean
water will add to the slight instability associated with the
system, bringing a convective element with embedded thunderstorms
to the rain. For this reason, rainfall rates of 0.5 to 0.65" an
hour are possible, especially for the northwest part of the
region, which could produce urban flooding, small stream rises,
and small rockfalls to the mountain regions. The front will lose
energy as it moves inland and gets farther from the ocean, so
rates are expected to diminish as it moves in southern OC/IE and
into San Diego Co. 

Rainfall will taper off quite quickly behind the main band, which
will move out of OC and the IE around 3-4 PM and out of San Diego
County by about 6 PM. Another wave or so of off-and-on rain will
follow behind, but rain will be much lighter with very little
chance for any thunderstorms. Snow levels start fairly high with 
the main precipitation at above 7500 feet, though heavier 
precipitation could locally drive this down to about 7000 feet. 
Snow levels drop behind the front to about 7000 feet late Thursday
afternoon, then to about 6000 feet late Thursday night. The
majority of snow is expected above the communities/main roads on
the ridges, though a few inches at the resort level and on the
high mountain passes is expected. Rain will likely transition to
snow later Thursday in Big Bear, but with wet, heavy snow we're
not expecting a lot in the way of accumulation, around 0.1" to
about an inch.

&&

.LONG TERM...Fri Nov 20 to Wed Nov 25...A few showers will linger
in southwest San Diego County through Friday morning, before the
weather dries and skies clear. Another shortwave trough rotates
through the region on the east side of the larger trough Friday,
but this will mostly just keep us cooler than average. This is
followed by a brief period of ridging Saturday, though this will
be weak and transient enough that temperatures will only bump up a
few degrees for Saturday afternoon. 

Another weak shortwave follows late Sunday into Monday. This has a
moderate chance (~40% chance) of bringing some more precipitation
to the region, though this would be much, much lighter. A handful
of global ensemble members are still showing mostly dry weather,
so confidence in the forecast for next week is moderate. Another
brief ridge is likely late Monday into Tuesday, before another low
pressure system looms towards late Tuesday-Wednesday. This latter
system has trended slightly wetter, with more ensemble members
showing precipitation than previous runs, but there are large
differences in strength, timing, and depth of troughing that will
make huge differences in the temperature, rain, etc. forecast for
next week.

.KEY MESSAGES...

* Precipitation is expected through tonight, with wintry 
  conditions at elevations at or above 4000 feet, especially in 
  Siskiyou County 

* Activity eases on Thursday with east side snow showers tapering
  off, ahead of a break Friday into Saturday morning

* Frost/freeze concerns will be considered for the Umpqua Valley 
  and some coastal areas

* Active weather looks to return later Saturday, and continue for
  much of the next week, but impacts at this time look 
  low/limited

&&

.DISCUSSION...

A closed 500mb low continues to pass through the region today. 
This is the main driver for today's ongoing precipitation albeit 
most has tapered off as of writing this, especially any impactful
amounts. Precipitation is anticipated to continue tonight with 
additional snowfall across higher elevation areas of northern 
California and eastside areas. Overall, not expecting much in the 
realm of impacts, but slippery roads will certainly be possible 
through Thursday morning. Thereafter, we are looking at a break in
activity as far as potential impacts goes.

By Saturday morning, another upper level trough will pass through
the region. This is our next chance at seeing impacts from snow 
and rain. Initially, snow levels are low Saturday morning 
currently forecast around 1600ft for eastside areas, but as low as
2000ft for some westside areas. This is before the QPF really 
gets going. At this time, we are not expecting low level valley 
floor snowfall, but these lower snow levels definitely caught our
eye. Once the QPF starts to ramp up, snow levels do rise, and a 
majority of the snowfall is anticipated around or above 5000ft. 
This could be a 48 hour "event" with precipitation from Saturday 
morning through Monday morning. Given snowfall at these higher 
elevations, we may not see much impacts from this system, but we 
still have time to refine these details if anything changes. For 
now, only expecting low/limited impacts with that second system. 

Next week, the upper levels remain active as we continue this 
sinusoidal pattern with wave after wave over the PacNW. Next week
is Thanksgiving, and one of the busiest travel weeks, so we are 
definitely monitoring things closely. At this time, it does 
appear additional snowfall will be possible as early as Tuesday 
but impacts look to be once again low/limited given accumulation 
above 4500 feet. Stay tuned as we refine details around 
Thanksgiving which is still about 8 days out. 

&&

.AVIATION (18Z TAFs)...

Rain and snow showers will bring impacts to the terminals through
this cycle with a IFR and MVFR conditions common. Overnight, 
confidence was high enough to introduce LIFR ceilings for westside
valleys from residual low level saturation impacting both KRBG

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Reno NV
1213 PM PST Wed Nov 18 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

* A potent winter storm continues to impact the region through 
  Friday morning, bringing heavy Sierra snow, strong winds, and 
  hazardous travel.

* Strong winds will continue over Sierra ridges, with gusty winds
  across western Nevada valleys and northeast California.

* A brief break in precipitation Friday afternoon through Saturday
  morning will be followed by another system arriving Saturday
  afternoon, with yet another system on Thanksgiving week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...

The active weather pattern continues as a deep Pacific trough 
impacts the region through Friday morning. Winter Storm Warnings 
remain in effect for the Sierra and northeastern California, with 
a Winter Weather Advisory for the Greater Reno-Carson City-Minden 
area.

In the Sierra, precipitation is already underway, with sites like
Truckee and South Lake Tahoe already reporting light snow. The 
heaviest snowfall rates are still expected to peak between 1-7 PM 
around Tahoe, and 6-11 PM for Mono County. Those peak snowfall 
rates are expected to be around 2-3 inches/hour. Snow showers will
continue through late Thursday night, though lingering showers 
may keep going in the Sierra through Friday morning. When the 
storm is all said and done by Friday morning, we'll be looking at 
1-2 feet of snow in the Tahoe Basin (higher amounts on the western
side), upwards of 4 feet along Donner Pass on I-80, 3-4 feet in 
Mammoth Lakes, 2-3 feet in June Lake, and 6-12 inches along US-395
in Mono County. Farther north, around 12 inches for Sierraville, 
Portola, and Beckwourth. For more detailed snow information, see 
the Avalanche discussion below.

Aside from light rain showers, the best chance for valley snow is
still anticipated late tonight into Thursday morning as snow 
levels drop below 5000 ft. This will likely impact the Thursday 
morning commute for many areas, with slick and icy conditions 
persisting even after precipitation ends. Total snow accumulations
in lower valleys and foothills outside of the Sierra are 1-4 
inches for the Sierra Front, 5-8 inches for Virginia City, 1-4 
inches for Cedarville, and 4-8 inches for Susanville. Amounts 
taper off fairly quickly once you get east of the Pine Nuts and 
the Virginia Range.

Strong winds will continue to be a significant hazard during this
storm, especially over Sierra ridges where gusts up to 90-100 mph
are still expected through Thursday. As for valley locations,
we've seen the winds gust into the 50-60 mph range across the
Sierra Front this morning, but those winds are expected to weaken
today as the precip moves in. Gusts across western NV and
northeast CA are forecast to remain in the 30-40 mph range before
2 PM today. 

Conditions will gradually ease by Friday morning with lingering 
showers, followed by clearing skies in the afternoon as the storm
system exits to the east. Very cold temperatures are expected 
Friday night and Saturday morning with lows dropping into the 
single digits and teens for many mountain and valley locations. 
For example, Reno's low temperature Saturday morning is expected 
to be around 10-13 degrees, and into the single digits for 
Truckee.

An active pattern is expected to continue across the West this
weekend and next week. Another trough will approach the West 
Coast late Saturday, bringing the next round of unsettled weather.
NBM guidance shows increasing chances of snow returning to the 
Sierra and western Nevada by Saturday night and continuing through
Sunday and Monday. This system appears to be less potent than the
current one, with lower precipitation totals, but will maintain 
colder-than-average temperatures across the region.

Another, potentially more impactful, trough is forecast to move 
into the West next week (Tuesday into Wednesday), bringing 
potential for more significant snowfall to northern California and
the Sierra. Model agreement on the exact timing and strength of 
this system is still variable, but the overall trend points to a 
continued active weather pattern through Thanksgiving week.

-Justin

&&

.AVIATION...

KRNO Forecast: Light rain continues this afternoon with a 10-30% 
of a rain snow mix with the strongest showers resulting in very 
light snow accumulations, if any at all. Rain/snow mix chances 
increase to 30-50% between 00Z-03Z with rain turning to snow 
between 04-06Z. MVFR to IFR conditions are expected due to lower 
CIGs and VIS associated with the showers. Mountain obscurations 
prevail through the period. There is a 30-50% chance of seeing an 
1+ inch of snow tomorrow. Winds of 30+ mph are expected through 
01-03Z this evening, then slowly decreasing through the night. 
LLWS and turbulence continues through tomorrow.

Regional Outlook: For KTRK/KTVL periods of snow have started 
leading to MVFR to LIFR conditions reducing CIGs and VIS. Snow 
accumulations over 15 inches are likely (60-80%) through Friday 
morning. KMMH will have similar accumulations but periods of snow 
will start later today. For the rest of the western NV sites, the 
KRNO forecast above applies to them. LLWS and turbulence as well 
as mountain obscurations are expected at all sites through 
tomorrow.

24-72 Hour Outlook: Heavy mountain snow and valley rain/snow 
showers taper off by Friday morning. The next system approaches on
Saturday afternoon and evening bringing more valley rain and 
mountain snow.

-HC

.AVALANCHE...

An early season winter storm system will bring heavy snow to all 
avalanche center terrain through Friday AM. 

* Snowfall Totals and Rates: Expect 2-4 feet of snow above 7000

  snowfall rates will occur today and Thursday afternoons and 
  evenings at 2-3 inches per hour. 

* SWE, SLRs, and Snow Levels: Along the crest, SWE of 3-3.25 inches 
  with 1.5-2.5 inches elsewhere. SLRs will be relatively high at 11-

* Ridgetop Wind Gusts and Thunder: Southwest winds gusting over

  snow bands could produce locally higher snowfall rates up to 4

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Las Vegas NV
349 PM PST Wed Nov 18 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

* A low pressure system will bring snow to the mountains of Inyo 
  County and southern Nevada beginning today and continuing 
  through Friday morning. 

* This low pressure system will also bring gusty southerly-to-
  southwesterly wind to the region over the next few days.

* There will be a brief reprieve from unsettled weather over the
  weekend before the next system impacts the area early next week. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...through Wednesday.

Current satellite imagery shows a closed upper-low pushing down the 
Pacific Northwest coast. This system will continue to dig southeast 
over the next 24 to 36 hours, bringing unsettled weather to 
southeastern California, southern Nevada, and northwestern Arizona 
through Friday. Latest radar also shows a wide area of precipitation 
pushing into central California with areas of moderate to heavy 
rain, along with snow for the higher elevations. As the day goes on, 
precipitation will increase over the southern Sierra, bringing 
widespread snow to the eastern Sierra this afternoon through 
Thursday morning. The bulk of the heavier snow is forecast to fall 
in the Sierra, where 3 to 4 feet is possible for the higher 
elevations and 2 to 3 feet for areas like Aspendell (8,400 feet). 
Even elevations between 6,000 and 8,000 feet could see around a foot 
of snow. A Winter Storm Warning remains in effect for the Eastern 
Sierra through Friday morning and looks to be on track. Rain is 
expected in the Owens Valley with totals generally between 0.50" and 
1.00" by Thursday evening. Precipitation amounts will drop off 
further east, though the White Mountains could still see a few 
inches of snow, where a Winter Weather Advisory is in effect through 
Friday morning.

The main band of precipitation is projected to push east early 
Thursday morning, continue through the day, and exit the area 
Thursday night. Valley rainfall amounts will remain generally light 
outside of Inyo County, with most areas seeing less than a tenth of 
an inch. In the Spring Mountains, a Winter Weather Advisory is in 
effect from 4:00 AM PST Thursday through early Friday morning. For 
elevations between 7,000 and 9,500 feet, storm-total snow 
accumulations of 3 to 9 inches are forecast. Looking specifically at 
the Mount Charleston and Lee Canyon areas, 4 to 8 inches looks to be 
the most likely scenario, with a 10% chance of seeing 10 inches or 
greater.

In addition to the mountain snow and valley rain, this system will 
bring gusty south to southwest winds today and Thursday. The 
strongest winds today will remain confined to the northwest 
CWAincluding Inyo, Esmeralda, and central and southern Nye 
countieswhere sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph and gusts to 45 mph 
are expected. Wind Advisories are in effect for these areas from 
4:00 PM this afternoon through Thursday morning. As the system 
pushes east, gusty winds will develop Thursday afternoon through 
Thursday evening across San Bernardino, southern Clark, and Mohave 
counties, with gusts between 40 and 45 mph prompting additional Wind 
Advisories. Expect difficult driving conditions for high-profile 
vehicles, and use extra caution as blowing dust near dry lakebeds 
may reduce visibility.

Conditions will improve throughout the day Friday into Saturday as 
the trough exits the region. While temperatures will remain cooler 
than normal through the weekend, weak, transient ridging will 
provide a brief reprieve from the precipitation and wind. This quiet 
stretch will be short-lived, however, as another system looks to 
impact the region early next week.

&&

.AVIATION...For Harry Reid...For the 00Z Forecast Package...Easterly 
winds will weaken after sunset and remain variable through the 
evening. Winds start to favor a northwesterly direction through most 
of the morning with speeds under 10 knots. Southwesterly winds pick 
up in the afternoon with speeds of 10 knots or greater and gusts to 
around 20 knots. Precipitation also starts to enter the valley 
starting late morning. The greatest potential for rainfall at the 
terminal is between 21Z and 00Z. Ceilings may fall to as low a 6kft 
during the heaviest precipitation. 

For the rest of southern Nevada, northwest Arizona and southeast
California...For the 00Z Forecast Package...Breezy winds decrease 
and cloud cover continues to increase across most of the region 
tonight. Precipitation moves in from west to east throughout the day 
tomorrow and gusty southwesterly to westerly winds pick up in the 
afternoon. Ceilings fall to the 4 to 6kft range with the rainfall. 
At KBIH, Gusty southerly to southeasterly winds, rainfall, and OVC 
ceilings persist for most of the forecast period. Cloud bases drop 
to the 1 to 3kft range starting at 09Z through the end of the TAF 
period. rainfall is unlikely along the Colorado River Valley 
including KEED and KIFP.

&&

.SPOTTER INFORMATION STATEMENT...Spotters are encouraged to report
any significant weather or impacts according to standard operating
procedures.

&&

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Phoenix AZ
250 PM MST Wed Nov 18 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Overall quiet weather conditions are expected through the rest
  of the week with dry conditions and temperatures at or just
  below normal.

- A couple of passing weather systems, one Thursday into Friday
  and another next Monday, should bring breezy conditions and
  periods of clouds, but any chances of precipitation are expected
  to be across northern Arizona and on the windward side of the
  southern California mountains.

&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Under clear skies overnight, low temperatures reached their
coldest since February-early March of this year. Most lower
desert locations fell into the 40s this morning and some valleys
and higher elevation locations dipped into the 30s. Flagstaff fell
to around 20F. Synoptically, zonal flow is currently seen over the
area with 573-576dam H5 heights. Conditions are also much drier
after yesterday's cold front. Surface dew points are in the 30s
and 40s. Overall, it will be a very pleasant Fall afternoon with
plenty of sun, very light winds, and slightly below normal 
temperatures with afternoon highs topping out in the upper-60s to 
lower-70s.

Heading into Thursday and Friday a large low pressure system will
slowly work its way across the West. Models remain in excellent
agreement keeping the bulk of the cyclonic circulation just to 
the north of the local area. A weak to moderate AR will work south
through CA Thursday, reaching SoCal by midday and the afternoon, 
but cross-section forecast analysis shows most of the moisture 
with this AR will be below 700mb. So, just about all of this 
moisture will be squeezed out on the windward side of the SoCal 
mountains and Southeast CA will be rain shadowed with no 
indication of an AR besides some cumulus and wave clouds Thursday 
afternoon and evening. Not much moisture will make it into the 
southern AZ deserts either, but still just enough PBL moisture for
some lower cumulus Friday morning as the moisture axis pushes 
across AZ. Latest NBM PoPs remain below 5% for nearly all areas of
south-central AZ through southeast CA Thursday afternoon through 
midday Friday.

Temperatures will get a brief boost on Thursday with highs back 
into the mid 70s before cooler air moves through Thursday night 
into Friday dropping highs into the upper 60s to the lower 70s. 

&&

.LONG TERM /SATURDAY THROUGH NEXT WEEK/...
The active weather pattern affecting mostly the northern tier 
states will continue through the weekend into next week. After the
weather system affects mostly the Great Basin on Friday ejects to
the east on Saturday, weak upper level ridging is favored to 
eventually move over the Desert Southwest lasting through the 
rest of the weekend. The cooler air behind the system will 
however be hard to move out of the region. Below normal 
temperatures are forecast for the weekend with Saturday's highs 
mostly in the upper 60s to right around 70 degrees Sunday. 
Overnight lows will also take a decent dip with lower desert 
readings falling into the 40s. Many higher terrain areas should 
also see lows well into the 30s this weekend with the coldest air 
and lows dipping below freezing across much of the northern 
Arizona high country.

Model spread increases enough for early next week to put some
doubt in what will happen with a potential weak disturbance that
may move through or near our region on Monday. At the moment, the
GEFS somewhat favors some sort of a weak and mostly dry system 
moving through, while the EPS favors an even faster and weaker
shortwave bypassing us to the north but holding back a deeper
trough off the West Coast. No matter the eventual solution, very
little moisture is expected to move through our region and this is
reflected in the less than 10% PoPs over the lower deserts to at
most 10-20% for the higher terrain. NBM forecast temperatures also
favor steady-state readings, but if model trends favor the EPS we
may see temperatures rise back closer to 75 degrees for highs.
Looking out even further, ensembles favor a more significant ridge
building along and off the West Coast later next week. If this
holds true, we should see temperatures rise to above normal for 
the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

&&

.AVIATION...Updated at 1713Z.

South Central Arizona including KPHX, KIWA, KSDL, and KDVT: 
No aviation concerns are expected through the current TAF period.
Very light winds, generally aob 7 kt, will favor familiar diurnal
trends through the morning hours before taking on a more uncommon
N/NNW component by the afternoon and then redeveloping the typical
E component overnight. Extended periods of VRB conditions are
likely to be seen given the weaker-than-normal speeds. A FEW
passing cirrus decks will be seen over the region through this
evening before coverage increases during the overnight hours.

Southeast California/Southwest Arizona including KIPL and KBLH: 
No aviation concerns are expected during the next 24 hours. Very
weak winds, with speeds generally aob 7 kt, will be common through
the next 24 hours. Extended periods of VRB conditions are likely
given the weak flow. Winds at KIPL may tend to exhibit more of a
SE component this afternoon and evening and a SW component 
overnight. At KBLH, winds may tend to exhibit a S/SE component 
this afternoon and evening. A FEW passing high clouds will be seen
over the region through this afternoon before coverage increases 
this evening.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER... 
Dry air will persist across the region through much of the next
7 days with MinRHs mostly between 20-35%. Light winds will also 
return for today, before another weather system moves through the 
region Thursday and Friday. This system is not expected to bring 
any precipitation, but it will bring another bout of gusty winds 
and reinforce cooler temperatures. Winds then become light again
this weekend.

&&

.HYDROLOGY...
Gila: A Flood Warning remains in effect from Painted Rock Dam 
through the Dateland area due to water releases from the dam. 
Water releases remain around 3000 cfs. This will have the 
potential to flood farm fields and low water crossings along the 
river downstream from the dam.

&&

CA...None.
&&

$$

Day 1 Fire Weather Outlook  
NWS Storm Prediction Center Norman OK
1035 AM CST Wed Nov 18 2026

Valid 181700Z - 191200Z

The ongoing forecast remains on track for an Elevated fire weather
threat across the CO Front Range and portions of the central Plains
today. 16z surface observations depict sustained wind speeds of
15-25 mph and gusts up to 40-50 mph within the risk area, and RH
values have declined to near 15% in the CO Front Range. Satellite
imagery portrays some mid/high cloud cover near the cold front
positioned over western NE, but is expected to clear out as the
front translates eastward. Winds will begin to wane after 21z as the
shortwave trough and surface low exit the region; however,
coinciding 20-25% RH and gusty winds amid pockets of dormant/cured
fine fuels will maintain increased fire weather concerns in the
central Plains for a few afternoon hours.

..Elizalde-Garcia.. 11/18/2026

.PREV DISCUSSION... /ISSUED 1151 PM CST Tue Nov 17 2026/

...Synopsis...
A negatively-tilted upper trough and attendant mid-level jet will
eject into the central and northern Plains today. A related
deepening surface low will translate northeastward towards the
ND/Canadian border by tonight. A surface anticylone over the Mid
Atlantic will be accompanied by an upper ridge over the eastern U.S.
leading to warm and dry conditions for the region.

...Colorado Front Range and portions of the Central Plains... 
Strong, post-post frontal westerly winds of 25-35 mph with gusts to
50 mph will evolve through the morning hours across southeastern WY
and much of western NE. Downslope drying will yield RH as low as 10%
along and adjacent to the CO Front Range with the strongest winds
displaced farther north across southeastern WY/western/central NE
where RH reductions will be limited to between 20% and 25%. The
central High Plains have observed several days of sub-freezing
temperatures since early November which has contributed to pockets
of dormant/cured fine fuels across the region, although the overall
fuelscape lacks critical dryness necessary for more significant
wildfire growth. Elevated highlights have been introduced into
portions of southeastern WY, western/central NE and southward along
and east the CO Front Range for the increased fire weather concerns
where they align with drier fuels.

Broad surface high pressure across the eastern U.S. will promote
warming temperatures and dry conditions across much of the Southeast
and into the Appalachians where fuels are notably dry. Weak surface
pressure gradients will promote light winds, limiting the overall
fire weather threat within this region.

...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov/fire for graphic product...

Day 2 Fire Weather Outlook  
NWS Storm Prediction Center Norman OK
0131 PM CST Wed Nov 18 2026

...NO CRITICAL AREAS...

Fire weather concerns will remain low across the CONUS on Day
2/Thursday. Surface high pressure residing over the Mid-Atlantic
will maintain dry conditions as daytime high temperatures rise into
the mid-to-upper 60s. Minimum RH values will range from 20-30%

limit a significant fire weather threat across the region.

The upper trough over the central plains on D1/Wednesday will
quickly move northeastward into the Great Lakes by D2/Thursday while

will persist across the central High Plains as southerly winds
return in the presence of lee surface troughing. South winds of
10-15 mph (locally 20 mph) combined with RH as low as 10% during

weather concerns will remain limited with an attenuated fuelscape
across the region.

Fuels will continue to deteriorate within the Appalachians as high
pressure remains over the eastern U.S., although the light wind
regime will continue to limit fire weather concerns for D2/Thursday.

National Weather Service / California-Nevada RFC / Sacramento CA
105 PM PST Wed Nov 18 2026

...HEAVIEST PRECIP MOVES FROM I-80 CORRIDOR SOUTHWARD WED PM-THU...
...WEAKER SYSTEM ANTICIPATED THIS WEEKEND FOR NORTHERN CA...

.METEOROLOGICAL CONDITIONS (WED PM - TUE AM)...

Heaviest precip associated with the slow moving cold front is 
currently impacting areas along the I-80 corridor from the SF Bay 
Area northeast across the Sacramento area...eventually reaching the 
west slope of the Sierra. Precip gauges for just 2 hours ending at 
18/20Z are showing several gauges through the SF Bay Area nearing or 
surpassing the 1.00-inch mark...including Downtown San Francisco 
(1.19-inches) and Oakland Airport (0.95-inch)...and this should 
translate inland along the I-80 corridor as the current 6-hour 
period progresses to 19/00Z. 

For this evening...look for the heaviest precip to shift across the 
central/southern Sierra back to the Big Sur Coast. Then for the 
overnight precip will make its way to the far southern Sierra and 
back southwest to the Point Conception area. Looking at 
probabilities for 2.00-inches or more during a 6-hour period...the 
18/12Z REFS continues to pinpoint areas along the coast from 
Monterey County down across San Luis Obispo County this 
evening...and then again tomorrow morning as the frontal boundary 
rounds Point Conception and brings moderate to heavy precip along 
the transverse mountains of Santa Barbara and Ventura counties. 

While the frontal boundary continues to shift inland and south 
across the region...models have been steady in showing a mid-level 
disturbance along with a sfc low tracking over the SF Bay Area and 
then past the Sacramento area up I-80 to near Lake Tahoe before 
weakening across northern NV. This should bring an uptick to precip 
tomorrow morning through the afternoon hours in these locations. The 
frontal boundary will finally begin to weaken after bringing 
moderate to heavy precip across the remainder of the transverse 
ranges over to southwest San Bernardino County...resulting in lesser 
totals for the San Diego area. 

Friday looks to be a relatively quiet day across the region as the 
system from today and Thursday shifts to the east...and a brief 
transitory upr ridge slides across the area. Models are still not 
completely dialed into a system approaching the coast for this 
weekend into early next week...but looking at the 18/12Z EC and 
GFS...a slightly weaker solution is more likely. The latest 19/18Z 
NBM and WPCQPF does show a downward trend...and the afternoon 
forecast issuance followed this trend as well.

www.cnrfc.noaa.gov/Daily-Briefing for a graphical summary of
weather and hydrologic conditions.
